lessons.title: Trace checkout across service boundaries and transactions
lessons.overview: Order is an orchestration boundary: it owns carts, checkout and chef-specific order state while resolving customer address facts from User-Chef and current menu/kitchen facts from Catalog. A multi-kitchen checkout becomes one parent checkout plus one order per kitchen. Engineers must understand which calls are reads from another source of truth, which facts are copied into immutable snapshots, and which writes participate in the local database transaction.

steps.label: Start at OrderController
steps.detail: Identify customer-scoped routes, authenticated identity and the request DTO that enters checkout.

steps.label: Trace external reads
steps.detail: Follow address validation to User-Chef and active menu/kitchen resolution to Catalog.

steps.label: Trace grouping
steps.detail: Locate how cart lines are grouped by kitchen and how parent/child identifiers are established.

steps.label: Trace snapshots
steps.detail: Identify pickup, drop-off, item and package facts copied at checkout so later profile edits do not rewrite history.

steps.label: Trace chef lifecycle
steps.detail: Follow ChefOrderController and service behavior for acceptance, preparation timing, rejection and readiness.

steps.label: Mark side effects
steps.detail: Separate persisted order transitions from outbox/integration effects such as notifications, payment or delivery scheduling.

lessons.example: If Kitchen A and Kitchen B are in the same cart, a new fulfilment field may need to live on each chef-specific order, not only on the parent checkout, because the kitchens progress independently.
lessons.lab: Trace a synthetic two-kitchen checkout from OrderController to OrderService and the persisted parent/child structure. Mark every external lookup and every value that becomes an immutable snapshot.
lessons.pitfall: Do not reconstruct an existing order from current Catalog or profile data when the order already owns a historical snapshot.

questions.prompt: Why does checkout copy address and package facts into the order boundary?
options: To create a catalog search index
questions.explanation: Snapshots prevent later source edits from rewriting the historical order.

questions.prompt: Where should kitchen-specific fulfilment state normally live?
questions.explanation: Each kitchen order is an independent fulfilment boundary.

lessons.title: Add an order capability without breaking idempotency or history
lessons.overview: Order features are state-machine changes, not simple CRUD. Define which object owns the state, which prior states permit the action, whether the action may be retried, what historical facts must be stored, and which downstream services need a new contract. Implement the transition in the service layer inside an appropriate transaction, use a durable idempotency key for externally repeatable commands, and emit side effects only from an accepted transition.

steps.label: Choose the aggregate
steps.detail: Decide whether the feature belongs to cart, parent checkout, chef-specific order or scheduled-order state.

steps.label: Define transition rules
steps.detail: Write allowed source states, resulting state and invalid/repeated behavior before coding.

steps.label: Persist historical facts
steps.detail: Store values that must survive later profile/catalog edits rather than re-querying mutable sources later.

steps.label: Make retries safe
steps.detail: Use the existing command/idempotency pattern so network retries do not create duplicate transitions or side effects.

steps.label: Publish downstream effects
steps.detail: Trigger payment, notification or delivery integration only after the local state transition is durably accepted.

steps.label: Update clients/contracts
steps.detail: Change admin/customer/chef UI only after the order API and state semantics are covered by tests.

lessons.example: For an approved new chef-order status, define exactly which current states may enter it, record its timestamp if historically relevant, and make duplicate requests return the existing state instead of replaying downstream work.
lessons.lab: Design a generic approved chef-order transition. Produce a state table, idempotency rule, persistence fields, downstream event behavior, API response and negative tests.
lessons.pitfall: Do not add a status value to an enum and assume the feature is complete; transitions, persistence, consumers and rollback all need alignment.

questions.prompt: What is the first design artifact for a new order state?
questions.explanation: Order behavior must define legal state transitions before implementation.

questions.prompt: When should a downstream side effect be emitted?
options: After the owning order transition is durably accepted
questions.explanation: Side effects should follow an accepted local state transition.

lessons.title: Validate concurrency, retries and cross-service failures
lessons.overview: Order tests need to simulate failure at boundaries: address lookup unavailable, catalog item changed, duplicate checkout request, concurrent chef action, downstream notification failure and payment/delivery callbacks arriving more than once. The expected result must preserve a coherent order state. Release validation should include at least one real contract-level smoke across Order and its affected dependencies, while rollback must remain compatible with orders already written by the new version.

steps.label: Test dependency failure
steps.detail: Verify checkout fails or recovers according to contract when required User-Chef/Catalog facts cannot be obtained.

steps.label: Test duplicate commands
steps.detail: Repeat the same synthetic command and assert no duplicate parent order, child order or side effect appears.

steps.label: Test concurrent transitions
steps.detail: Submit competing chef/order actions and confirm only valid state movement wins.

steps.label: Test snapshots
steps.detail: Edit source profile/catalog data after checkout and confirm the existing order remains historically stable.

steps.label: Smoke integrations
steps.detail: Validate the exact affected payment/notification/delivery contract, not merely Order health.

steps.label: Plan compatible rollback
steps.detail: Ensure an older service can safely read orders created during the new release or keep the new schema backward compatible.

lessons.example: If a release writes a new nullable order field and then must be rolled back, the older code should be able to ignore that field. A destructive rollback migration is usually riskier than a compatible code rollback.
lessons.lab: Build a test matrix for a two-kitchen checkout with dependency failure, duplicate submit, one chef accept, one chef reject and repeated downstream signals. Define the expected persisted state after each case.
lessons.pitfall: Health endpoints cannot prove transactional correctness under duplicate or concurrent order commands.

questions.prompt: Which test best validates checkout idempotency?
options: Repeat the same command and verify no duplicate order graph
questions.explanation: Idempotency is proven by repeated equivalent commands producing one durable effect.

questions.prompt: What should rollback consider after new orders have been written?
options: Backward readability of newly written data
questions.explanation: Rollback code must remain compatible with data created by the newer version.
